content: Tinea versicolor is a chronic fungal infection of the skin. It is caused by the yeast Pityrosporum ovale, which is normally present on human skin but becomes problematic under certain conditions. The primary symptom of tinea versicolor is the appearance of discolored patches on the skin. These patches have well-defined edges and are often covered with fine scales. The patches are typically reddish-tan in color and are most commonly found on the back, underarms, upper arms, chest, and neck. Affected areas of the skin do not tan when exposed to sunlight, which can make them appear lighter than the surrounding healthy skin. In individuals with darker skin tones, such as African Americans, the condition may result in either hypopigmentation (loss of skin color) or hyperpigmentation (increased skin color). Other symptoms may include increased sweating and itching. Tinea versicolor is most commonly seen in adolescent and young adult males, particularly in hot climates. Diagnosis is confirmed by examining a skin scraping under a microscope, which reveals the presence of the yeast. Treatment involves the application of antifungal medications directly to the skin. Commonly used antifungal agents include clotrimazole, ketoconazole, and miconazole. Over-the-counter dandruff shampoos, when applied to the skin for 10 minutes daily during a shower, may also be effective in treating the condition. Although tinea versicolor is easily treatable, changes in skin pigmentation may persist for several months after treatment. The condition has a tendency to recur, especially during warm and humid months. Individuals with a history of tinea versicolor are advised to minimize exposure to excessive heat and sweating to help prevent recurrence. If symptoms develop, it is important to schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider for evaluation and management.
